newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain and China all smiles on 1997 handover.
newsitem.headline: Britain and China all smiles on 1997 handover.

text.p: Hong Kong governor Chris Patten and China's top official in the British colony were all smiles on Monday, papering over differences as the territory prepares for the handover to Chinese rule in 1997.
Patten and Zhou Nan, head of Beijing's de facto embassy here, shook hands, clinked glasses, and exchanged toasts for the first time in a year when they met to celebrate China's national day holiday.
The greeting suggested a new warmth in Sino-British relations following several years of bitter wrangling which China has blamed on Patten's unilateral expansion of democracy in the colony.
Beijing has vowed to dismantle Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council after the handover and replace it with a provisional legislature.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 next year.
Zhou acknowledged the improvement of relations between the two countries, expressing hopes that there would be no fresh troubles in the coming months.
"Some improvements have been made in Sino-British relations," he said.

"We hope that in the last few months of transition, both sides will abide by the provisions of the Sino-British Joint Declaration, better cooperate in matters concerning Hong Kong's smooth transition and the smooth transfer of government and that there will not be any new troubles," he said.
The joint declaration spells out the agreement on the handover.
The Chinese mandarin then toasted Britain's Queen Elizabeth and Patten.

Sino-British relations have showed signs of mending in recent months after Britain and Chinese negotiators reached agreements on contentious issues such as the handover ceremony, mobile phone licences and infrastructure projects.

Zhou said cooperation had also spread to Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp, which China has long regarded as "subversive". "We have noticed that some people who once went astray have begun to change," he said. He did not say how.

The Chinese enovy was confident that the resumption of Hong Kong sovereignty would be carried out according to plan, but he warned the next three months would be a crucial period as Patten and the Legislative Council's successors would be named by the end of this year.
Patten confined much of his speech to praising the economic success of both Hong Kong and China in recent years and avoided contentious issues like democracy.
He said the handover would be an important day for Hong Kong, Britain and China.
"No event in many years will have a greater impact on what the world expects from China and, perhaps, what China expects from the world," he said.

Several dozen anti-communist demonstrators staged a protest at the doorstep of the reception hall, shouting slogans and waving banners saying "End of dictatorship", "Set free the political prisoners" and "Set free (jailed dissident) Wei Jiangsheng".
They also hurled insults at those attending the event for implicitly backing the June 4, 1989, crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square when Chinese troops killed pro-democracy demonstrators.
